title: Can Language Models Learn When to Abstain? Policy Learning and Calibrated Answer Selection

paper.title: Can Language Models Learn When to Abstain? Policy Learning and Calibrated Answer Selection
paper.abstract: Abstract A useful language model should know when to answer and when to say “I don’t know.” Can we improve that decision by training the model itself or by training a separate component to check its answers? We study both approaches in Qwen3-14B on factual questions, using a score that rewards correct answers, penalizes mistakes, and permits abstention. Across three training seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds, a learned answer selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the original model’s calibrated confidence filter. On TriviaQA, mean coverage increases from 20.2% to 30.9%, while the pooled error rate among scored answers decreases from 23.0% to 14.5% under exact-match grading. The tested reinforcement-learning changes do not establish consistent gains. On NQ-Open, the selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the filter but remains below always abstaining. A partial human-reviewed audit preserves the TriviaQA finding. Our results support learning to select answers in this setting while showing that reliable abstention across datasets remains unresolved.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Language models can give plausible answers even when they lack the knowledge to answer correctly. For factual question answering, admitting uncertainty is often more useful than guessing. Yet a scoring rule that rewards correct answers and gives the same score to mistakes and abstentions encourages guessing: any chance of being correct is better than leaving a question unanswered. Penalizing mistakes changes this incentive [ 1 ] . Prior work shows that models can be trained to express uncertainty and that their confidence can help identify which answers to trust [ 2 , 5 ] . The practical challenge is to make abstention selective. A model that refuses every question avoids mistakes but provides no answers. One approach trains the answering model to choose between a response and an abstention. Another keeps the answering model fixed and uses a separate selector to decide whether to show its answer. Existing evidence does not determine which intervention will be useful for a particular model and compute budget. In our setting, the questions are whether training improves on a calibrated confidence filter, whether the model responds to confidence thresholds absent from training, and whether improvements survive a change of dataset. We investigate these questions with Qwen3-14B [ 30 ] . We compare controlled reinforcement-learning interventions with a learned answer selector, using three training seeds, two held-out confidence thresholds, and separate TriviaQA and NQ-Open tests. Our contribution is a comparison of these choices under a documented local training budget, with inexpensive controls and an audit of automatic grading. The clearest result is that the selector increases mean coverage and reduces pooled selective risk on TriviaQA relative to the original calibrated filter, aggregating the two primary thresholds. The RL comparisons remain inconclusive, and the selector does not establish positive utility on NQ. Together, these findings distinguish progress in answer selection from evidence of reliable abstention across datasets. The source code, experimental configurations, aggregate results, and reproduction instructions are publicly available at https://github.com/jrterven/Can-LLMs-learn-to-abstain .

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Abstention in language models involves factual reliability, confidence estimation, and decisions under uncertainty. We review the literature that informs our comparison of policy learning and answer selection, beginning with hallucinations and the signals used to identify unreliable responses. We then discuss selective prediction and methods for learning uncertainty and abstention, followed by the calibration concepts and evaluation metrics needed to assess the tradeoff between answering more questions and reducing errors.

sections.heading: 2.1 Hallucinations and factual reliability
sections.text: Hallucination encompasses several failures of language generation. Huang et al. [ 9 ] distinguish factuality errors, which conflict with verifiable world knowledge, from faithfulness errors involving the supplied context or instructions. TruthfulQA [ 10 ] illustrates how models can reproduce familiar human misconceptions. These distinctions matter for abstention: an incorrect response need not arise from random guessing, and a confident response need not be factually correct. Our experiments concern short factual answers without retrieval. An exact-match failure can also reflect a valid answer missing from the reference aliases [ 6 ] ; it therefore does not by itself establish a hallucination or identify its cause. Several detection methods use agreement across generated responses. SelfCheckGPT [ 11 ] checks the factual consistency of independently sampled passages without consulting an external knowledge base. Farquhar et al. [ 12 ] estimate semantic entropy by grouping answers with equivalent meanings, targeting arbitrary incorrect generations termed confabulations. Consistent systematic errors can escape agreement-based detection. These methods motivate uncertainty-based filtering, while using different evidence from the single question–candidate pair scored by our test-time selectors.

sections.heading: 2.2 Confidence estimation and selective prediction
sections.text: Kadavath et al. [ 5 ] study P(True), in which a model assesses whether a proposed answer is correct. Lin et al. [ 13 ] show that fine-tuning can teach models to express useful probability estimates in words. Xiong et al. [ 14 ] evaluate confidence elicitation across tasks and distinguish probability calibration from failure prediction, finding that verbal confidence is often overconfident and that elicitation strategies have uneven benefits. These results motivate evaluating a confidence signal empirically rather than treating its numerical value as a reliable probability. The answer-or-abstain decision is an instance of selective prediction. Chow [ 15 ] formalizes the error–reject tradeoff, and Geifman and El-Yaniv [ 16 ] study coverage and selective risk for deep classifiers. In QA, Kamath et al. [ 17 ] train a calibrator to predict errors and show that raw model confidence can be unreliable under domain shift. Their calibrator benefits from observing known out-of-domain examples; ours is fitted on TriviaQA and transferred to NQ without refitting. Conformal abstention [ 18 ] provides a related route to controlling the marginal probability of releasing an incorrect answer under exchangeability assumptions. That marginal error probability differs from the conditional error rate among released answers. Our empirical logistic calibration does not provide a comparable finite-sample guarantee after a dataset change.

sections.heading: 2.3 Learning uncertainty and abstention
sections.text: R-Tuning [ 2 ] constructs supervised examples around a model’s apparent knowledge boundary to teach uncertainty expression. Its analyses also use the trained uncertainty model to score answers from a separate generator. Both training an answering policy and learning which answers to release therefore have established precedents. SaySelf [ 19 ] combines supervised fine-tuning on self-reflective rationales with reinforcement learning to improve expressed confidence. Its training target emphasizes confidence estimates; our policy experiments directly score the answer-or- IDK decision. TruthRL [ 3 ] trains answering models with a ternary reward for correct answers, abstentions, and errors. Its main experiments use a fixed reward scheme, a model-based correctness verifier, and different data and optimization settings, so its gains are not a direct benchmark for our runs. Jha et al. [ 20 ] also vary abstention rewards and supervised initialization, reporting exploration limitations in open-ended tasks. At inference time, I-CALM [ 21 ] combines elicited verbal confidence, announced answer/abstain payoffs, and instructions favoring truthful responses. These approaches motivate comparing policy updates with inexpensive prompting and answer selection under a common evaluation rule. They do not determine which intervention will improve a particular model within the training budget used here.

sections.heading: 2.4 Calibration and evaluation metrics
sections.text: Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed correctness frequencies [ 22 ] . Logistic calibration maps a scalar score to a probability, following the sigmoid-fitting approach associated with Platt scaling [ 23 ] . Learning a more informative score, calibrating that score, and applying a release threshold are distinct operations. We separate them through raw and calibrated original-model scores, a learned selector, and a logistic control with access to the selector’s training labels. Coverage and selective risk describe the availability and reliability of released answers [ 16 , 17 ] ; cost-sensitive utility additionally accounts for the requested penalty for errors [ 15 , 1 ] . For confidence diagnostics, ROC AUC measures the ranking of correct above incorrect candidates [ 24 ] , while the binary Brier score measures squared probability prediction error [ 25 ] . Brier score reflects both calibration and resolution, so an improvement cannot be attributed to calibration alone [ 26 ] . Section 3.5 defines these measures and their evaluation populations before reporting results. AbstentionBench [ 27 ] considers several reasons to withhold an answer, including missing information and false premises. Our benchmark questions have reference answers, but the model may not reliably produce them. Kalai et al. [ 1 ] motivate explicit error penalties so that acknowledging uncertainty can be preferable to guessing. Kamalloo et al. [ 6 ] show that lexical grading can reject semantically valid QA responses, motivating our partial audit. The present contribution is a controlled empirical comparison of established policy-training and selection choices, with held-out thresholds, shared candidates for selector comparisons, cross-dataset evaluation, and a measured local training budget.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: We compare two routes to selective factual question answering: updating the policy that generates an answer or abstention, and learning whether to release an answer from a fixed generator. Figure 1 summarizes both routes. Starting from the same Qwen3-14B model, we train four controlled RL variants and compare three scoring approaches on shared candidate answers. Separate training and calibration partitions support learning and probability estimation, while held-out thresholds and a second dataset test how the resulting decisions generalize. We evaluate decision utility and answer reliability, quantify uncertainty across questions and training seeds, and examine sensitivity to automatic grading through a partial human-reviewed audit. The following subsections specify the decision rule, data, interventions, and evaluation protocol. Figure 1: Two routes to selective factual question answering. (a) A Qwen3-14B LoRA policy learns to answer or emit IDK ; the training reward uses κ = τ \kappa=\tau in arms A–C and κ = 0.75 \kappa=0.75 in arm D. (b) A frozen generator supplies identical candidates y ^ \hat{y} to three alternative scorers. Each score is calibrated on held-out TriviaQA data, and a valid candidate is released only if p ^ > τ \hat{p}>\tau ; calibration transfers unchanged to NQ. Reference answers provide training, calibration, and evaluation labels; they are absent from generation and scoring inputs.

sections.heading: 3.1 Task and decision rule
sections.text: The task is short factual question answering in English. The system receives a question and a requested confidence threshold τ \tau . It must either provide a brief answer or abstain with exactly IDK . A larger threshold makes an incorrect answer more costly. We use the same scoring rule to evaluate all methods and, where specified below, to train the answering model: R τ = c − τ ​ a = { 1 − τ correct answer , − τ incorrect answer , 0 abstention . R_{\tau}=c-\tau a=\begin{cases}1-\tau&\text{correct answer},\\ -\tau&\text{incorrect answer},\\ 0&\text{abstention}.\end{cases} (1) Here c c indicates a correct answer and a a indicates a scored answer, whether correct or incorrect. For example, at τ = 0.85 \tau=0.85 , a correct answer earns 0.15, a mistake loses 0.85, and abstention earns zero. If the probability of correctness is p p , answering has expected score p − τ p-\tau . It is therefore preferable to abstaining when p > τ p>\tau . This rule provides an incentive; it does not ensure that the model knows its true probability of success. Correctness is determined by normalized exact matching against reference aliases. Empty or truncated direct outputs count as errors. For filters, invalid candidates and candidates already abstaining are rejected. The answering model receives no references, retrieved documents, or search results. All threshold prompts use two fixed demonstrations and request a brief answer or IDK . Prompts used to generate candidates for filtering instead request a best short answer. Appendix F gives the exact message templates and score-calibration settings.

sections.heading: 3.2 Model, data, and training budget
sections.text: All trained models start from the same original Qwen3-14B revision, with extended thinking disabled and no earlier adapters or supervised warmup. We use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 31 ] to update a small set of parameters. Experiments run on one NVIDIA GB10 with approximately 128 GB of unified memory; implementation settings are in Appendix D . The training pool contains 2,000 TriviaQA questions, with separate development and calibration sets of 500 questions each. The tests contain 2,000 additional TriviaQA validation questions [ 7 ] and 500 NQ-Open Original Dev questions [ 8 , 32 ] . Fixed hashes select test questions after excluding IDs and normalized question texts used in earlier study partitions or demonstrations. These tests are new within our study; this does not establish absence of pretraining contamination. Earlier experiments that motivated this design are summarized separately in Appendix A . Policy training uses thresholds { 0.60 , 0.75 , 0.90 } \{0.60,0.75,0.90\} . The primary tests use { 0.65 , 0.85 } \{0.65,0.85\} , which were absent from policy training. A separate diagnostic panel uses the same 200 fixed questions within each dataset at all six thresholds { 0.60 , 0.65 , 0.75 , 0.85 , 0.90 , 0.95 } \{0.60,0.65,0.75,0.85,0.90,0.95\} , including the training thresholds and the additional held-out value 0.95 (Appendix E ). We use three training seeds, 17, 29, and 43, and retain the final checkpoint from every run. No recipe, seed, or checkpoint is selected on the test results. A timing check before test access reduced the RL training panel uniformly from 1,008 to 504 questions. Each RL run uses 252 updates and 12,096 generated responses. The selector uses the full 2,000-question training pool and 500 updates. Training budgets are matched within the RL comparisons; the selector is a different training procedure, not a budget-matched RL ablation.

sections.heading: 3.3 Training the answering model
sections.text: The RL approach changes how the model generates its answer or abstention. We test two training choices: how many sampled responses are compared when calculating the learning signal, and whether each question is practiced under one or several thresholds. A fixed-cost control tests whether making the reward depend on the requested threshold adds value. For each question, all four arms have three training exposures, with eight sampled responses per exposure. In A and B, the assigned threshold is repeated; in C and D, each training threshold appears once. A divides the eight responses into two groups of four for the reward baseline, whereas B–D compare all eight together. Thus the group-size comparison changes the baseline, not the number of generated responses. The baseline subtracts the mean reward of the other responses in the group, following leave-one-out methods used in LLM reinforcement learning [ 4 ] . Its equation and loss settings are in Appendix D . sections.heading: 3.4 Selecting answers from a fixed generator
sections.text: The selection approach leaves answer generation unchanged. The original model produces a candidate answer, and a separate scoring step estimates whether that candidate is correct. The candidate is shown only if its calibrated probability exceeds τ \tau ; otherwise the system returns IDK . All selection methods receive identical greedy test candidates. The inexpensive baseline uses the original model’s P(True) score, obtained by asking it to assess a candidate answer’s correctness [ 5 ] . Let ℓ True \ell_{\mathrm{True}} and ℓ False \ell_{\mathrm{False}} be the next-token logits after the question–candidate scoring prompt. We compute z = ℓ True − ℓ False , p raw = σ ⁡ ( z ) , p ^ = σ ⁡ ( α ​ z + β ) , z=\ell_{\mathrm{True}}-\ell_{\mathrm{False}},\qquad p_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sigma(z),\qquad\hat{p}=\sigma(\alpha z+\beta), (2) where σ ⁡ ( t ) = 1 / ( 1 + e − t ) \sigma(t)=1/(1+e^{-t}) . The raw score normalizes probability over the two tokens True and False ; it is not a generated numerical confidence statement. Logistic regression fitted on the 500 calibration question–candidate pairs learns α \alpha and β \beta , using the logit difference z z as its input, following sigmoid score calibration [ 23 , 22 ] . We compare the raw and calibrated probabilities to separate score calibration from learning a new scorer. For the learned selector, the original generator produces one greedy and three sampled candidates for each training question, giving 8,000 examples. A separate LoRA adapter learns their exact-match correctness from the question and candidate alone. It uses binary cross entropy on the difference between the True and False logits. The three selector runs share these examples and each train for one epoch, with 500 updates at learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} . Each selector is then calibrated on the separate calibration set by fitting its own α \alpha and β \beta to its learned logit difference in Equation 2 . Neither its scoring input nor the generator’s input contains reference answers. A further control fits logistic regression to the original logit differences using the same 8,000 training labels and then recalibrates its transformed logits. This control, labeled TRAIN logistic in the tables, tests the value of those labels when applied to the same fixed scalar score. Its two affine logit transformations compose to one affine transformation, so it cannot learn new question–candidate features; fitting data and regularization can still change its parameters. It matches the available labels, not model capacity or training cost. Appendix F specifies the fitting procedure. All calibration is learned on TriviaQA and transferred to NQ without refitting.

sections.heading: 3.5 Evaluation and uncertainty
sections.text: We evaluate the answer–abstain decision using utility, coverage, and selective risk. Coverage and selective risk are standard complementary measures in selective prediction: they describe how often a system answers and how frequently those answers are wrong [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . For N N questions at a fixed threshold τ \tau , let C C and E E count correct answers and errors under the output-format rules above. The three measures are U τ = ( 1 − τ ) ​ C − τ ​ E N , Coverage = C + E N , Risk = E C + E . U_{\tau}=\frac{(1-\tau)C-\tau E}{N},\qquad\operatorname{Coverage}=\frac{C+E}{N},\qquad\operatorname{Risk}=\frac{E}{C+E}. (3) Utility is the mean score in Equation 1 ; higher values are better. Coverage quantifies the fraction of questions receiving a scored answer, while lower selective risk indicates more accurate answers within that subset. Always abstaining has zero utility and zero coverage; its selective risk is undefined. At a fixed threshold and positive coverage, U τ = Coverage ⁡ ( 1 − Risk − τ ) U_{\tau}=\operatorname{Coverage}(1-\operatorname{Risk}-\tau) , so positive utility requires the correctness rate of scored answers to exceed the threshold. Utility is computed at each requested threshold before averaging; the fixed-threshold identity should not be applied to pooled coverage and risk using the mean threshold. When pooling evaluations, we divide total errors by total scored answers rather than average their risk percentages; format errors from direct generation are included in that denominator. We additionally assess the confidence scores using two candidate-level diagnostics before the release threshold is applied. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) measures how well a score ranks correct candidates above incorrect ones [ 24 ] . With correctness as the positive class, the ROC curve plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as the score threshold varies. Its area equals the probability that a randomly chosen correct candidate receives a higher score than a randomly chosen incorrect candidate, counting ties as one half; larger values indicate better ranking. The binary Brier score measures the squared error of a predicted probability of correctness [ 25 ] : Brier = 1 M ​ ∑ i = 1 M ( p ^ i − y i ) 2 , \operatorname{Brier}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}(\hat{p}_{i}-y_{i})^{2}, (4) where y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1\} is the exact-match correctness label, p ^ i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \hat{p}_{i}\in[0,1] is the evaluated probability estimate, and M M is the number of eligible candidates. Lower values indicate better probability predictions. The Brier score reflects both calibration and the ability to distinguish outcomes, so a reduction does not by itself demonstrate improved calibration [ 26 ] . Both diagnostics use the same valid, non-abstaining candidates across scoring methods, rather than only the answers each method releases. They are descriptive measures of score quality, complementary to utility at the requested operating thresholds. Five TriviaQA comparisons were specified before test evaluation: the three RL contrasts and the selector against each calibrated baseline (original filter and TRAIN logistic). We average utility over the two primary thresholds within each question, then construct intervals using 10,000 paired bootstrap replicates [ 28 ] . Each replicate independently resamples question indices and the three training-seed indices with replacement, using the same draws for both methods in a contrast. Pairing across the two thresholds is preserved by averaging them before resampling. The deterministic baseline is shared across seeds. The 99% intervals provide nominal 95% coverage for the five-comparison family using the Bonferroni correction [ 29 ] , subject to the bootstrap approximation. NQ comparisons and ordinary 95% intervals are descriptive. The intervals condition on the shared training candidate bank and fitted calibrators; three seeds give limited information about training variability.

sections.heading: 3.6 Audit of automatic grading
sections.text: After the main evaluation, we audited 150 response units from 144 questions: 100 candidates shared by the filters and 50 RL responses, with 75 units per dataset. A unit is identified by its question, exact response text, and truncation flag. Sampling was stratified by automatic label and filter-decision pattern. The form hid condition identities and automatic labels, but displayed reference aliases. ChatGPT proposed labels, and one annotator reported personally reviewing every label. This is AI-assisted human review, not agreement between two independent annotators. We assess sensitivity by applying reviewed labels to identical units across methods and primary thresholds. All other outputs retain exact-match labels. Output-format rules, generated answers, scores, calibrators, and release decisions stay fixed. For unresolved labels, we enumerate consistent correct/error assignments shared across all occurrences of a unit. Bootstrap intervals are conditional on the reviewed labels and sampled units; they exclude annotation and audit-sampling uncertainty. This partial analysis supplements the original endpoint and does not estimate semantic accuracy over the whole test set.

sections.heading: 4 Results
sections.text: We evaluate both approaches at the confidence thresholds held out from policy training, τ = 0.65 \tau=0.65 and τ = 0.85 \tau=0.85 . The main results use exact-match grading. Utility and coverage are averaged over the two thresholds and, for trained methods, all three seeds. Selective risk is computed by dividing the total number of errors by the total number of scored answers. Always abstaining gives zero utility, which provides a reference for assessing whether the methods benefit from answering.

sections.heading: 4.2 Reinforcement learning and computational cost
sections.text: The mean utility differences on TriviaQA are positive for all three RL comparisons: increasing the comparison group from four to eight responses gives a utility difference of 0.00827 (B–A), training each question at all three thresholds gives 0.01027 (C–B), and making the reward depend on the requested threshold gives 0.03578 (C–D). However, all three adjusted intervals include zero, and the direction of the differences varies across seeds (Figure 2 ). For C–D, for example, the 99% interval is [ − 0.02240 , 0.08424 ] [-0.02240,0.08424] . The recorded experiments take 35.44 hours of serial task time, including pilots, model loading, candidate preparation, training, evaluation, and CPU analysis. The later audit analysis and human annotation are excluded. At inference, both the confidence filters and the learned selector require a scoring step after answer generation. Appendix C provides the time breakdown.

sections.heading: 4.3 Effect of the partial human review
sections.text: The review of 150 response units yields 104 correct answers, 19 errors, 24 abstentions, and three unclear cases. Forty responses marked as errors by exact matching are judged semantically correct: 21 in TriviaQA and 19 in NQ. The review confirms all 64 responses originally marked correct and all 24 abstentions. Because the sample is stratified, these counts do not estimate the grading error rate for the full test sets. All three unclear cases are in NQ. Treating each as either correct or incorrect gives eight possible label assignments for the sensitivity analysis. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: The strongest evidence concerns which answers to show. Across the two primary thresholds, the learned selector improves mean utility and coverage while reducing pooled selective risk on the same TriviaQA candidates. This supports better answer selection at the aggregate operating point. The RL experiments address a different mechanism: they change both the generated answers and the abstention decisions. Their training data and costs also differ from the selector’s. The table, therefore, compares practical outcomes, while the matched RL contrasts and shared-candidate filter comparisons support the narrower inferences reported above. The inconclusive RL results do not show that reinforcement learning cannot teach abstention. One difficulty follows from the reward itself: if every sampled response is an answer, changing τ \tau subtracts the same constant from all rewards, so centering removes that cost signal (Appendix D ). This motivates examining response diversity and optimization but does not identify the cause of the observed seed variability. TruthRL uses a different training and verification setup [ 3 ] ; its success does not establish that one change would repair our recipe. A historical local semantic judge also failed challenge checks and was not adopted (Appendix A ). Transfer and grading limit the conclusions. NQ shows that improved confidence ranking can coexist with negative observed utility when calibration is learned on another dataset. The audit also shows that exact-match labels can reject valid answers and may affect both training and evaluation. Correcting the reviewed cases preserves the TriviaQA selector advantage, but the remaining responses have not been reviewed semantically. One person’s review of AI-proposed labels, with reference aliases visible, is not an independently replicated factual verification. The study covers one model family, short English QA, and three seeds. Shared training candidates and calibrators are not resampled in the intervals. The logistic control is cheaper and less expressive than the selector; an arm with groups of four and exposure to all three training thresholds would also be needed to estimate the full interaction between the two RL interventions. The protocol was frozen locally, not externally preregistered. Any future recipe chosen after these results will require a new test set for independent confirmation.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusions
sections.text: In this study, learning which answers to show gives the clearest improvement in useful abstention. Aggregating the two primary thresholds, a calibrated selector increases mean coverage and reduces pooled exact-match selective risk on TriviaQA relative to the original calibrated filter; its utility advantage remains after the observed audit corrections. The tested RL interventions remain inconclusive. On NQ, neither better confidence scores nor the partial corrections establish an advantage over always abstaining. These findings support answer selection under the tested distribution and leave reliable transfer as an open empirical problem.

sections.heading: Appendix F Prompt templates and calibration
sections.text: The message templates below reproduce the generator and scorer inputs. Role prefixes identify chat-message roles and are not additional prompt text. Braces mark substitutions: {question} is the question, {candidate_answer} is the proposed answer, and {tau:.2f} is the requested threshold formatted with two decimal places. sections.heading: F.1 Threshold-conditioned answer generation
sections.text: The same two demonstrations are used for every threshold-conditioned question. Only the requested threshold and final question change. System: You answer factual questions. System: Judge whether the proposed answer is factually correct for the question. Reply only True or False. sections.heading: F.4 Calibration fits and the TRAIN logistic control
sections.text: All logistic fits use L2 regularization with C = 1 C=1 , the lbfgs solver, at most 1,000 iterations, and random_state=0 . Each learned selector fits its own calibration map on that same partition. Fitting uses all 500 labeled pairs; the release rule subsequently rejects invalid or already-abstaining candidates. The descriptive Brier and AUC populations in Table 3 exclude those candidates. Each of the four candidates for a training question receives weight 1 / 4 1/4 , so each question has total weight one. The first fit changes the input scale seen by the regularized second fit, so their estimated probabilities need not be identical. Policy Learning and Calibrated Answer Selection Juan Terven Affiliation: CICATA Qro., Instituto Politécnico Nacional, México Diana-Margarita Córdova-Esparza Affiliation: Facultad de Informática, Universidad Autónoma de Querétaro, México Ruben Gomez Affiliation: CICATA Qro., Instituto Politécnico Nacional, México Carlos Miranda Rocha Affiliation: Facultad de Informática, Universidad Autónoma de Querétaro, México Julio-Alejandro Romero-González Affiliation: Facultad de Informática, Universidad Autónoma de Querétaro, México Edgar Chavez-Urbiola Affiliation: CICATA Qro., Instituto Politécnico Nacional, México October 7, 2026 Abstract A useful language model should know when to answer and when to say “I don’t know.” Can we improve that decision by training the model itself or by training a separate component to check its answers? We study both approaches in Qwen3-14B on factual questions, using a score that rewards correct answers, penalizes mistakes, and permits abstention. Across three training seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds, a learned answer selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the original model’s calibrated confidence filter. On TriviaQA, mean coverage increases from 20.2% to 30.9%, while the pooled error rate among scored answers decreases from 23.0% to 14.5% under exact-match grading. The tested reinforcement-learning changes do not establish consistent gains. On NQ-Open, the selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the filter but remains below always abstaining. A partial human-reviewed audit preserves the TriviaQA finding. Our results support learning to select answers in this setting while showing that reliable abstention across datasets remains unresolved. 1 Introduction Language models can give plausible answers even when they lack the knowledge to answer correctly. For factual question answering, admitting uncertainty is often more useful than guessing. Yet a scoring rule that rewards correct answers and gives the same score to mistakes and abstentions encourages guessing: any chance of being correct is better than leaving a question unanswered. Penalizing mistakes changes this incentive [ 1 ] . Prior work shows that models can be trained to express uncertainty and that their confidence can help identify which answers to trust [ 2 , 5 ] . The practical challenge is to make abstention selective. A model that refuses every question avoids mistakes but provides no answers. One approach trains the answering model to choose between a response and an abstention. Another keeps the answering model fixed and uses a separate selector to decide whether to show its answer. Existing evidence does not determine which intervention will be useful for a particular model and compute budget. In our setting, the questions are whether training improves on a calibrated confidence filter, whether the model responds to confidence thresholds absent from training, and whether improvements survive a change of dataset. We investigate these questions with Qwen3-14B [ 30 ] . We compare controlled reinforcement-learning interventions with a learned answer selector, using three training seeds, two held-out confidence thresholds, and separate TriviaQA and NQ-Open tests. Our contribution is a comparison of these choices under a documented local training budget, with inexpensive controls and an audit of automatic grading. The clearest result is that the selector increases mean coverage and reduces pooled selective risk on TriviaQA relative to the original calibrated filter, aggregating the two primary thresholds. The RL comparisons remain inconclusive, and the selector does not establish positive utility on NQ. Together, these findings distinguish progress in answer selection from evidence of reliable abstention across datasets. The source code, experimental configurations, aggregate results, and reproduction instructions are publicly available at https://github.com/jrterven/Can-LLMs-learn-to-abstain . 2 Related Work Abstention in language models involves factual reliability, confidence estimation, and decisions under uncertainty. We review the literature that informs our comparison of policy learning and answer selection, beginning with hallucinations and the signals used to identify unreliable responses. We then discuss selective prediction and methods for learning uncertainty and abstention, followed by the calibration concepts and evaluation metrics needed to assess the tradeoff between answering more questions and reducing errors. 2.1 Hallucinations and factual reliability Hallucination encompasses several failures of language generation. Huang et al. [ 9 ] distinguish factuality errors, which conflict with verifiable world knowledge, from faithfulness errors involving the supplied context or instructions. TruthfulQA [ 10 ] illustrates how models can reproduce familiar human misconceptions. These distinctions matter for abstention: an incorrect response need not arise from random guessing, and a confident response need not be factually correct. Our experiments concern short factual answers without retrieval. An exact-match failure can also reflect a valid answer missing from the reference aliases [ 6 ] ; it therefore does not by itself establish a hallucination or identify its cause. Several detection methods use agreement across generated responses. SelfCheckGPT [ 11 ] checks the factual consistency of independently sampled passages without consulting an external knowledge base. Farquhar et al. [ 12 ] estimate semantic entropy by grouping answers with equivalent meanings, targeting arbitrary incorrect generations termed confabulations. Consistent systematic errors can escape agreement-based detection. These methods motivate uncertainty-based filtering, while using different evidence from the single question–candidate pair scored by our test-time selectors. 2.2 Confidence estimation and selective prediction Kadavath et al. [ 5 ] study P(True), in which a model assesses whether a proposed answer is correct. Lin et al. [ 13 ] show that fine-tuning can teach models to express useful probability estimates in words. Xiong et al. [ 14 ] evaluate confidence elicitation across tasks and distinguish probability calibration from failure prediction, finding that verbal confidence is often overconfident and that elicitation strategies have uneven benefits. These results motivate evaluating a confidence signal empirically rather than treating its numerical value as a reliable probability. The answer-or-abstain decision is an instance of selective prediction. Chow [ 15 ] formalizes the error–reject tradeoff, and Geifman and El-Yaniv [ 16 ] study coverage and selective risk for deep classifiers. In QA, Kamath et al. [ 17 ] train a calibrator to predict errors and show that raw model confidence can be unreliable under domain shift. Their calibrator benefits from observing known out-of-domain examples; ours is fitted on TriviaQA and transferred to NQ without refitting. Conformal abstention [ 18 ] provides a related route to controlling the marginal probability of releasing an incorrect answer under exchangeability assumptions. That marginal error probability differs from the conditional error rate among released answers. Our empirical logistic calibration does not provide a comparable finite-sample guarantee after a dataset change. 2.3 Learning uncertainty and abstention R-Tuning [ 2 ] constructs supervised examples around a model’s apparent knowledge boundary to teach uncertainty expression. Its analyses also use the trained uncertainty model to score answers from a separate generator. Both training an answering policy and learning which answers to release therefore have established precedents. SaySelf [ 19 ] combines supervised fine-tuning on self-reflective rationales with reinforcement learning to improve expressed confidence. Its training target emphasizes confidence estimates; our policy experiments directly score the answer-or- IDK decision. TruthRL [ 3 ] trains answering models with a ternary reward for correct answers, abstentions, and errors. Its main experiments use a fixed reward scheme, a model-based correctness verifier, and different data and optimization settings, so its gains are not a direct benchmark for our runs. Jha et al. [ 20 ] also vary abstention rewards and supervised initialization, reporting exploration limitations in open-ended tasks. At inference time, I-CALM [ 21 ] combines elicited verbal confidence, announced answer/abstain payoffs, and instructions favoring truthful responses. These approaches motivate comparing policy updates with inexpensive prompting and answer selection under a common evaluation rule. They do not determine which intervention will improve a particular model within the training budget used here. 2.4 Calibration and evaluation metrics Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed correctness frequencies [ 22 ] . Logistic calibration maps a scalar score to a probability, following the sigmoid-fitting approach associated with Platt scaling [ 23 ] . Learning a more informative score, calibrating that score, and applying a release threshold are distinct operations. We separate them through raw and calibrated original-model scores, a learned selector, and a logistic control with access to the selector’s training labels. Coverage and selective risk describe the availability and reliability of released answers [ 16 , 17 ] ; cost-sensitive utility additionally accounts for the requested penalty for errors [ 15 , 1 ] . For confidence diagnostics, ROC AUC measures the ranking of correct above incorrect candidates [ 24 ] , while the binary Brier score measures squared probability prediction error [ 25 ] . Brier score reflects both calibration and resolution, so an improvement cannot be attributed to calibration alone [ 26 ] . Section 3.5 defines these measures and their evaluation populations before reporting results. AbstentionBench [ 27 ] considers several reasons to withhold an answer, including missing information and false premises. Our benchmark questions have reference answers, but the model may not reliably produce them. Kalai et al. [ 1 ] motivate explicit error penalties so that acknowledging uncertainty can be preferable to guessing. Kamalloo et al. [ 6 ] show that lexical grading can reject semantically valid QA responses, motivating our partial audit. The present contribution is a controlled empirical comparison of established policy-training and selection choices, with held-out thresholds, shared candidates for selector comparisons, cross-dataset evaluation, and a measured local training budget. 3 Methodology We compare two routes to selective factual question answering: updating the policy that generates an answer or abstention, and learning whether to release an answer from a fixed generator. Figure 1 summarizes both routes. Starting from the same Qwen3-14B model, we train four controlled RL variants and compare three scoring approaches on shared candidate answers. Separate training and calibration partitions support learning and probability estimation, while held-out thresholds and a second dataset test how the resulting decisions generalize. We evaluate decision utility and answer reliability, quantify uncertainty across questions and training seeds, and examine sensitivity to automatic grading through a partial human-reviewed audit. The following subsections specify the decision rule, data, interventions, and evaluation protocol. Figure 1: Two routes to selective factual question answering. (a) A Qwen3-14B LoRA policy learns to answer or emit IDK ; the training reward uses κ = τ \kappa=\tau in arms A–C and κ = 0.75 \kappa=0.75 in arm D. (b) A frozen generator supplies identical candidates y ^ \hat{y} to three alternative scorers. Each score is calibrated on held-out TriviaQA data, and a valid candidate is released only if p ^ > τ \hat{p}>\tau ; calibration transfers unchanged to NQ. Reference answers provide training, calibration, and evaluation labels; they are absent from generation and scoring inputs. 3.1 Task and decision rule The task is short factual question answering in English. The system receives a question and a requested confidence threshold τ \tau . It must either provide a brief answer or abstain with exactly IDK . A larger threshold makes an incorrect answer more costly. We use the same scoring rule to evaluate all methods and, where specified below, to train the answering model: R τ = c − τ ​ a = { 1 − τ correct answer , − τ incorrect answer , 0 abstention . R_{\tau}=c-\tau a=\begin{cases}1-\tau&\text{correct answer},\\ -\tau&\text{incorrect answer},\\ 0&\text{abstention}.\end{cases} (1) Here c c indicates a correct answer and a a indicates a scored answer, whether correct or incorrect. For example, at τ = 0.85 \tau=0.85 , a correct answer earns 0.15, a mistake loses 0.85, and abstention earns zero. If the probability of correctness is p p , answering has expected score p − τ p-\tau . It is therefore preferable to abstaining when p > τ p>\tau . This rule provides an incentive; it does not ensure that the model knows its true probability of success. Correctness is determined by normalized exact matching against reference aliases. Empty or truncated direct outputs count as errors. For filters, invalid candidates and candidates already abstaining are rejected. The answering model receives no references, retrieved documents, or search results. All threshold prompts use two fixed demonstrations and request a brief answer or IDK . Prompts used to generate candidates for filtering instead request a best short answer. Appendix F gives the exact message templates and score-calibration settings. 3.2 Model, data, and training budget All trained models start from the same original Qwen3-14B revision, with extended thinking disabled and no earlier adapters or supervised warmup. We use low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 31 ] to update a small set of parameters. Experiments run on one NVIDIA GB10 with approximately 128 GB of unified memory; implementation settings are in Appendix D . The training pool contains 2,000 TriviaQA questions, with separate development and calibration sets of 500 questions each. The tests contain 2,000 additional TriviaQA validation questions [ 7 ] and 500 NQ-Open Original Dev questions [ 8 , 32 ] . Fixed hashes select test questions after excluding IDs and normalized question texts used in earlier study partitions or demonstrations. These tests are new within our study; this does not establish absence of pretraining contamination. Earlier experiments that motivated this design are summarized separately in Appendix A . Policy training uses thresholds { 0.60 , 0.75 , 0.90 } \{0.60,0.75,0.90\} . The primary tests use { 0.65 , 0.85 } \{0.65,0.85\} , which were absent from policy training. A separate diagnostic panel uses the same 200 fixed questions within each dataset at all six thresholds { 0.60 , 0.65 , 0.75 , 0.85 , 0.90 , 0.95 } \{0.60,0.65,0.75,0.85,0.90,0.95\} , including the training thresholds and the additional held-out value 0.95 (Appendix E ). We use three training seeds, 17, 29, and 43, and retain the final checkpoint from every run. No recipe, seed, or checkpoint is selected on the test results. A timing check before test access reduced the RL training panel uniformly from 1,008 to 504 questions. Each RL run uses 252 updates and 12,096 generated responses. The selector uses the full 2,000-question training pool and 500 updates. Training budgets are matched within the RL comparisons; the selector is a different training procedure, not a budget-matched RL ablation. 3.3 Training the answering model The RL approach changes how the model generates its answer or abstention. We test two training choices: how many sampled responses are compared when calculating the learning signal, and whether each question is practiced under one or several thresholds. A fixed-cost control tests whether making the reward depend on the requested threshold adds value. For each question, all four arms have three training exposures, with eight sampled responses per exposure. In A and B, the assigned threshold is repeated; in C and D, each training threshold appears once. A divides the eight responses into two groups of four for the reward baseline, whereas B–D compare all eight together. Thus the group-size comparison changes the baseline, not the number of generated responses. The baseline subtracts the mean reward of the other responses in the group, following leave-one-out methods used in LLM reinforcement learning [ 4 ] . Its equation and loss settings are in Appendix D . The original model produces a candidate answer, and a separate scoring step estimates whether that candidate is correct. The candidate is shown only if its calibrated probability exceeds τ \tau ; otherwise the system returns IDK . All selection methods receive identical greedy test candidates. The inexpensive baseline uses the original model’s P(True) score, obtained by asking it to assess a candidate answer’s correctness [ 5 ] . Let ℓ True \ell_{\mathrm{True}} and ℓ False \ell_{\mathrm{False}} be the next-token logits after the question–candidate scoring prompt. We compute z = ℓ True − ℓ False , p raw = σ ⁡ ( z ) , p ^ = σ ⁡ ( α ​ z + β ) , z=\ell_{\mathrm{True}}-\ell_{\mathrm{False}},\qquad p_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sigma(z),\qquad\hat{p}=\sigma(\alpha z+\beta), (2) where σ ⁡ ( t ) = 1 / ( 1 + e − t ) \sigma(t)=1/(1+e^{-t}) . The raw score normalizes probability over the two tokens True and False ; it is not a generated numerical confidence statement. Logistic regression fitted on the 500 calibration question–candidate pairs learns α \alpha and β \beta , using the logit difference z z as its input, following sigmoid score calibration [ 23 , 22 ] . We compare the raw and calibrated probabilities to separate score calibration from learning a new scorer. For the learned selector, the original generator produces one greedy and three sampled candidates for each training question, giving 8,000 examples. A separate LoRA adapter learns their exact-match correctness from the question and candidate alone. It uses binary cross entropy on the difference between the True and False logits. The three selector runs share these examples and each train for one epoch, with 500 updates at learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} . Each selector is then calibrated on the separate calibration set by fitting its own α \alpha and β \beta to its learned logit difference in Equation 2 . Neither its scoring input nor the generator’s input contains reference answers. A further control fits logistic regression to the original logit differences using the same 8,000 training labels and then recalibrates its transformed logits. This control, labeled TRAIN logistic in the tables, tests the value of those labels when applied to the same fixed scalar score. Its two affine logit transformations compose to one affine transformation, so it cannot learn new question–candidate features; fitting data and regularization can still change its parameters. It matches the available labels, not model capacity or training cost. Appendix F specifies the fitting procedure. All calibration is learned on TriviaQA and transferred to NQ without refitting. 3.5 Evaluation and uncertainty We evaluate the answer–abstain decision using utility, coverage, and selective risk. Coverage and selective risk are standard complementary measures in selective prediction: they describe how often a system answers and how frequently those answers are wrong [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . For N N questions at a fixed threshold τ \tau , let C C and E E count correct answers and errors under the output-format rules above. The three measures are U τ = ( 1 − τ ) ​ C − τ ​ E N , Coverage = C + E N , Risk = E C + E . U_{\tau}=\frac{(1-\tau)C-\tau E}{N},\qquad\operatorname{Coverage}=\frac{C+E}{N},\qquad\operatorname{Risk}=\frac{E}{C+E}. (3) Utility is the mean score in Equation 1 ; higher values are better. Coverage quantifies the fraction of questions receiving a scored answer, while lower selective risk indicates more accurate answers within that subset. Always abstaining has zero utility and zero coverage; its selective risk is undefined. At a fixed threshold and positive coverage, U τ = Coverage ⁡ ( 1 − Risk − τ ) U_{\tau}=\operatorname{Coverage}(1-\operatorname{Risk}-\tau) , so positive utility requires the correctness rate of scored answers to exceed the threshold. Utility is computed at each requested threshold before averaging; the fixed-threshold identity should not be applied to pooled coverage and risk using the mean threshold. When pooling evaluations, we divide total errors by total scored answers rather than average their risk percentages; format errors from direct generation are included in that denominator. We additionally assess the confidence scores using two candidate-level diagnostics before the release threshold is applied. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) measures how well a score ranks correct candidates above incorrect ones [ 24 ] . With correctness as the positive class, the ROC curve plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as the score threshold varies. Its area equals the probability that a randomly chosen correct candidate receives a higher score than a randomly chosen incorrect candidate, counting ties as one half; larger values indicate better ranking. The binary Brier score measures the squared error of a predicted probability of correctness [ 25 ] : Brier = 1 M ​ ∑ i = 1 M ( p ^ i − y i ) 2 , \operatorname{Brier}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}(\hat{p}_{i}-y_{i})^{2}, (4) where y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1\} is the exact-match correctness label, p ^ i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \hat{p}_{i}\in[0,1] is the evaluated probability estimate, and M M is the number of eligible candidates. Lower values indicate better probability predictions. The Brier score reflects both calibration and the ability to distinguish outcomes, so a reduction does not by itself demonstrate improved calibration [ 26 ] . Both diagnostics use the same valid, non-abstaining candidates across scoring methods, rather than only the answers each method releases. They are descriptive measures of score quality, complementary to utility at the requested operating thresholds. Five TriviaQA comparisons were specified before test evaluation: the three RL contrasts and the selector against each calibrated baseline (original filter and TRAIN logistic). We average utility over the two primary thresholds within each question, then construct intervals using 10,000 paired bootstrap replicates [ 28 ] . Each replicate independently resamples question indices and the three training-seed indices with replacement, using the same draws for both methods in a contrast. Pairing across the two thresholds is preserved by averaging them before resampling. The deterministic baseline is shared across seeds. The 99% intervals provide nominal 95% coverage for the five-comparison family using the Bonferroni correction [ 29 ] , subject to the bootstrap approximation. NQ comparisons and ordinary 95% intervals are descriptive. The intervals condition on the shared training candidate bank and fitted calibrators; three seeds give limited information about training variability. 3.6 Audit of automatic grading After the main evaluation, we audited 150 response units from 144 questions: 100 candidates shared by the filters and 50 RL responses, with 75 units per dataset. A unit is identified by its question, exact response text, and truncation flag. Sampling was stratified by automatic label and filter-decision pattern. The form hid condition identities and automatic labels, but displayed reference aliases. ChatGPT proposed labels, and one annotator reported personally reviewing every label. This is AI-assisted human review, not agreement between two independent annotators. We assess sensitivity by applying reviewed labels to identical units across methods and primary thresholds. All other outputs retain exact-match labels. Output-format rules, generated answers, scores, calibrators, and release decisions stay fixed. For unresolved labels, we enumerate consistent correct/error assignments shared across all occurrences of a unit. Bootstrap intervals are conditional on the reviewed labels and sampled units; they exclude annotation and audit-sampling uncertainty. This partial analysis supplements the original endpoint and does not estimate semantic accuracy over the whole test set. 4 Results We evaluate both approaches at the confidence thresholds held out from policy training, τ = 0.65 \tau=0.65 and τ = 0.85 \tau=0.85 . The main results use exact-match grading. Utility and coverage are averaged over the two thresholds and, for trained methods, all three seeds. Selective risk is computed by dividing the total number of errors by the total number of scored answers. Always abstaining gives zero utility, which provides a reference for assessing whether the methods benefit from answering. 4.1 Answer selection on TriviaQA and NQ-Open The learned selector answers more TriviaQA questions with a lower error rate among the answers it returns (Table 2 ). Across the two primary thresholds, the learned selector improves mean utility and coverage while reducing pooled selective risk on the same TriviaQA candidates. This supports better answer selection at the aggregate operating point. The RL experiments address a different mechanism: they change both the generated answers and the abstention decisions. Their training data and costs also differ from the selector’s. The table, therefore, compares practical outcomes, while the matched RL contrasts and shared-candidate filter comparisons support the narrower inferences reported above. The inconclusive RL results do not show that reinforcement learning cannot teach abstention. One difficulty follows from the reward itself: if every sampled response is an answer, changing τ \tau subtracts the same constant from all rewards, so centering removes that cost signal (Appendix D ). This motivates examining response diversity and optimization but does not identify the cause of the observed seed variability. TruthRL uses a different training and verification setup [ 3 ] ; its success does not establish that one change would repair our recipe. A historical local semantic judge also failed challenge checks and was not adopted (Appendix A ). Transfer and grading limit the conclusions. NQ shows that improved confidence ranking can coexist with negative observed utility when calibration is learned on another dataset. The audit also shows that exact-match labels can reject valid answers and may affect both training and evaluation. Correcting the reviewed cases preserves the TriviaQA selector advantage, but the remaining responses have not been reviewed semantically. One person’s review of AI-proposed labels, with reference aliases visible, is not an independently replicated factual verification. The study covers one model family, short English QA, and three seeds. Shared training candidates and calibrators are not resampled in the intervals. The logistic control is cheaper and less expressive than the selector; an arm with groups of four and exposure to all three training thresholds would also be needed to estimate the full interaction between the two RL interventions. The protocol was frozen locally, not externally preregistered. Any future recipe chosen after these results will require a new test set for independent confirmation. 6 Conclusions In this study, learning which answers to show gives the clearest improvement in useful abstention. Aggregating the two primary thresholds, a calibrated selector increases mean coverage and reduces pooled exact-match selective risk on TriviaQA relative to the original calibrated filter; its utility advantage remains after the observed audit corrections. The tested RL interventions remain inconclusive. On NQ, neither better confidence scores nor the partial corrections establish an advantage over always abstaining. These findings support answer selection under the tested distribution and leave reliable transfer as an open empirical problem.
